practice_questions.text: Name the large round shield carried by a Greek hoplite.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: hoplon (accept aspis or shield).

practice_questions.text: Describe the Corinthian-type helmet dedicated at Olympia and explain what it reveals about hoplite warfare.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it enclosed most of the face / had a T- or Y-shaped opening; 1 mark for a specific detail (beaten from a single sheet of bronze / almost no decoration / signs of wear consistent with actual use); 1 mark for a valid point about what it reveals (designed for close-order fighting where limited vision was acceptable / dedicated at a Panhellenic sanctuary as a thank-offering, showing the religious dimension of victory).

practice_questions.text: Below is a summary of a description from an ancient source. A red-figure vase painting from the early fifth century BC shows a line of Greek soldiers advancing in close order. Each man carries a large round shield on his left arm and holds a long spear at his right side. The shields of adjacent figures overlap. Analyse this source as evidence for how the phalanx worked.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Uses specific details from the source (overlapping shields, spear-carrying, close order) to make analytical points about how the phalanx functioned; explains the significance of each detail (e.g. overlapping shields created a collective defensive wall; spears project forward to threaten the enemy); sustains analysis throughout with reference to named source material or broader context. Secure: Identifies relevant features and makes valid analytical points; some explanation of significance but may not sustain all points fully. Developing: Describes what is shown rather than analysing it; limited explanation of what the features reveal about the phalanx. Emerging: Simple observations about the source with little or no analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the cost of hoplite equipment was important for Greek society.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid point with explanation, up to 4: e.g. equipment was self-purchased so only men of moderate wealth could serve as hoplites / this created a link between property, military service and political status / those who could not afford the panoply served as lighter troops or rowers / in Athens the hoplite class (zeugitai) had greater political influence than the poorest citizens / the spread of hoplite warfare reflected and reinforced a middling-class political culture.

practice_questions.text: How far was the success of the phalanx due to its equipment rather than the discipline and training of the soldiers who used it? Use the sources you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument evaluating both factors; uses named sources (Corinthian helmet at Olympia, Warrior Vase, literary accounts); reaches a clear, supported judgement; writes as an argument, not a description. Secure: Clear argument addressing both equipment and discipline; uses some named sources; judgement present but may be less fully supported. Developing: Addresses the question with some relevant points on both sides; limited use of sources; judgement may be asserted rather than argued. Emerging: Simple description of equipment or training; little argument; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the term othismos and how it decided the outcome of a phalanx battle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the term clearly (the push of shields / the collision of two phalanxes) and develops a full account of how it worked and why it was decisive (rear ranks adding weight; the side that broke was destroyed; psychological and physical pressure); integrates named sources or examples. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail; some development but may not sustain all points. Developing: Basic explanation of the term; limited account of its significance. Emerging: Vague or incorrect explanation; little relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Name the German archaeologist who excavated Mycenae in 1876.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Heinrich Schliemann.

practice_questions.text: Describe the discovery Schliemann made inside Grave Circle A at Mycenae.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: he found shaft graves containing rich burial goods; gold death masks were found (including the one he called the Mask of Agamemnon); bronze swords and weapons were uncovered; amber beads and elaborate jewellery were found; the graves dated to roughly 1550–1500 BC.

practice_questions.text:
Read this account of Schliemann's discovery:

'Inside the graves he found golden vessels, elaborate jewellery, and the faces of the dead covered with thin masks of beaten gold. He was convinced he was looking at the remains of King Agamemnon himself.'

Using the account and your own knowledge, explain what this discovery tells us about the Mycenaean world.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: simple point about the gold objects or the identity claim, with little development.
Developing: uses one detail from the source (e.g. gold masks) and offers a basic comment about wealth or the link to Homer; may describe rather than analyse.
Secure: uses specific details from the source and connects them to knowledge of Mycenaean society (e.g. gold masks indicate elite status and funerary ritual; Schliemann's identification is questioned because the graves predate any historical Trojan War). Shows understanding of the source as evidence.
Mastering: analyses the source in detail, evaluates its significance and limitations (graves dated c.1550–1500 BC, three centuries before the traditional date of the Trojan War; Schliemann's identification was a romantic projection but the discovery nonetheless proved a real Bronze Age civilisation at Mycenae). Engages with what the evidence can and cannot tell us.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the collapse of the Mycenaean palace system is difficult for historians to explain.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following points (or 2 marks each for two well-developed points): the collapse happened across the eastern Mediterranean simultaneously, suggesting multiple causes rather than one event; proposed causes include invasion, internal rebellion, earthquake, drought and famine — but no single cause fits all sites; Linear B writing disappeared, removing textual records; the evidence at different sites varies (Mycenae shows destruction by fire; other sites were abandoned without evidence of violence); the tablets from Pylos suggest preparation for attack at one site only.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Homer's Odyssey gives us reliable evidence about the Mycenaean world? Use evidence from the poem and from material sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: a simple list of things Homer says with little evaluation.
Developing: some attempt to compare Homer with archaeology, but evidence is vague and the argument is not sustained.
Secure: a clear two-sided argument. The response identifies ways in which Homer appears to reflect Mycenaean reality (bronze weapons, palace feasting, great citadels, gift exchange) and ways in which it diverges (iron tools appear; the poems were composed centuries after the Bronze Age; details may be poetic invention). Named sources are used on both sides.
Mastering: a sophisticated, evaluative argument that reaches a supported judgement. The response discusses how the poems are layered oral traditions rather than documentary records; it uses specific examples (the boar’s tusk helmet in Iliad Book 10; the gold-rich palaces compared with Grave Circle A finds; Schliemann’s problematic identification). The conclusion is clear and earned by the argument.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why modern scholars doubt that the gold death mask found by Schliemann belonged to King Agamemnon.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of the following: the graves in Grave Circle A date to approximately 1550–1500 BC, roughly three centuries before the traditional date of the Trojan War; Agamemnon is a figure from myth and may not have existed as a historical person; archaeology cannot confirm the identity of the person buried; Schliemann's identification was based on his desire to link the finds to Homer, not on evidence.

practice_questions.text: Name the officer who commanded a century in the Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: centurion.

practice_questions.text: Describe the standard structure of a Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three, for example: a legion contained roughly 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers; it was divided into ten cohorts; each cohort was made up of six centuries of around eighty men; each century was commanded by a centurion; the first cohort was double-strength and held the place of greatest honour.

practice_questions.text:
Read this description of a Roman material source: a small bronze statuette, approximately 8 cm tall, showing a soldier standing in a relaxed pose. He wears segmented body armour over a tunic, carries a large rectangular shield, and on his head sits a helmet with cheek-guards. A short sword hangs from his right hip. The figure was found in Britain and is now in the British Museum (1867, 0510.4).

What does this source tell us about the Roman legionary in the Imperial period? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of specific features of the source (armour, shield, sword, helmet) linked to wider knowledge of the legion's equipment and organisation. The response considers what the source confirms and what it cannot tell us (e.g. it shows parade or off-duty dress, not necessarily battle formation). At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details from the source, linked to accurate knowledge of the legionary's role. Some consideration of what the source reveals or limits.
Developing: General reference to the source with limited specific detail; knowledge of the legion mainly descriptive.
Emerging: Minimal engagement with the source; knowledge vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why training and discipline were important to the success of the Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: rigorous weapons training meant soldiers could fight effectively in close order; heavy training weapons meant real equipment felt lighter in battle; the ability to march twenty miles and then build a camp gave the army strategic flexibility; severe punishments (flogging, decimation) maintained collective discipline and prevented cowardice; standardised training meant soldiers from different parts of the empire could fight together effectively.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the Roman fortress at Chester as evidence for understanding the Roman army in the Imperial period?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis weighing the site's specific strengths (regular layout revealing hierarchy and function, barracks showing how centuries were housed, presence of hospital and bathhouse indicating permanent settlement) against limitations (the site has been altered over time; we cannot know the day-to-day experience of soldiers from the architecture alone). Named features of the site are used precisely.
Secure: Clear discussion of what the fortress reveals, with some acknowledgement of limitations. Specific features are named.
Developing: Mainly descriptive account of the fortress with limited evaluative comment.
Emerging: Vague reference to the fortress; limited accurate knowledge.

practice_questions.text: How important was discipline to the Roman army? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that evaluates discipline as central to Roman military effectiveness, supported by specific evidence (training with the palus, punishment by flogging, decimation as collective terror, the aquila as a symbol demanding collective commitment). The response also considers discipline alongside other factors (professional pay and rewards, engineeering skills, modular organisation) and reaches a supported judgement on the relative importance of discipline. Named sources are integrated.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Some range of points; a supported conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points about discipline but limited range; explanation may be underdeveloped or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited or missing; may retell facts without argument.

practice_questions.text: Name the architectural order used in the construction of the Parthenon.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Doric (order).

practice_questions.text: Describe the main features of the cella of a Greek temple.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the cella was the inner chamber of the temple; it housed the cult statue of the god; it was generally inaccessible to ordinary worshippers; it was entered through the pronaos (entrance porch); it could contain a treasury; it was surrounded on the outside by columns (peristyle).

practice_questions.text: Read the following description of a famous Roman temple: a massive circular building entered through a Corinthian-columned porch, its interior covered by a concrete dome of exactly equal height and diameter, with a circular hole open to the sky at its very centre. What does this architectural design suggest about the Romans' attitude towards the gods and their skill as builders? Use details from the description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Precise reference to specific details in the description (dome, oculus, Corinthian porch, equal height and diameter) with sustained analysis of what each implies; the circular oculus linked to the open eye of heaven or the all-seeing gods; the dome's mathematical perfection linked to divine order; the concrete construction linked to Roman engineering ambition. A clear judgement about what the combination reveals.
Secure (3-4): Two or three specific details used analytically with some explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description without engaging with the source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the altar was placed outside a Greek or Roman temple rather than inside it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following developed points: the cella was the god's private dwelling and worship happened in the god's presence outside; the altar was the site of animal sacrifice which required open air (smoke, fire, blood); crowds could not fit inside the restricted cella; the god's statue stood inside as the permanent resident while the community gathered outside; Roman temples on a podium with frontal steps meant the altar directly faced the entrance steps.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Parthenon is the greatest achievement of Greek architecture? Use named sources and a balanced argument in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained argument engaging with the Parthenon's specific features (Doric order, entasis, Pheidias' cult statue, sculptural programme, Pentelic marble) alongside comparison with at least one other major Greek structure; balanced view considering what makes architecture 'greatest' (innovation, beauty, scale, religious function); judgement clearly supported by named sources.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument with reference to the Parthenon's features and at least one comparator; some awareness of different criteria; evidence cited.
Developing (3-5): Some relevant points about the Parthenon with limited comparison or limited source use.
Emerging (1-2): Simple descriptive points; little or no argument or source use.

practice_questions.text: Explain two key differences between Greek and Roman temple design.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Greek peripteral colonnade vs Roman engaged columns + podium; Greek temples approachable from all sides vs Roman frontal entrance; use of concrete and dome in Rome vs marble column-and-lintel in Greece) with specific named examples for each (Parthenon / Temple of Portunus / Pantheon) and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about each culture's priorities.
Secure (3-4): Two differences identified and explained with some evidence but analysis less developed.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

practice_questions.text: Name the Greek poet who tells the story of Pandora in Works and Days.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Hesiod.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens when Pandora opens the jar in Hesiod's account.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: all evils and sicknesses are released into the world; the jar (pithos) had previously kept these evils contained; only Hope remains inside the jar; Pandora acts out of curiosity; the opening of the jar is the origin of human suffering in Hesiod's myth.

practice_questions.text: Read the following summary of a passage from Euripides' Medea (lines 1–38): The Nurse speaks, describing how Medea brought disaster on herself by falling in love with Jason and using her skills to help him. She now sits motionless, staring at the ground, weeping. She neither eats nor lifts her eyes. The Nurse fears what Medea might do. Using this passage and your wider knowledge, analyse what this source reveals about the character of Medea and what she represents to an Athenian audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): The student uses specific details from the summary (Medea's stillness, tears, refusal to eat) to analyse her character as consumed by passionate emotion. They connect this to her identity as a foreigner and sorceress, explaining why an Athenian audience would find her threatening — she operates outside the social controls placed on Athenian women. The student may discuss how the Nurse's fear signals Medea's dangerous unpredictability. Named source cited accurately.

Secure (3–4): The student identifies relevant details from the passage and makes points about Medea's emotional extremity and threat. Some connection to wider cultural context. Named source used.

Developing (2): Some relevant points made but largely narrative or descriptive. Limited use of specific source details.

Emerging (1): A simple point with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the story of the Sabine Women was important to the Romans.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any four of the following, up to a maximum of 4:
1 mark for each point: the myth provided an origin for the Roman population and its mixture with the Sabines; the Sabine women's intervention embodied Roman female virtues of loyalty and self-sacrifice; the myth justified early Roman expansion and acquisition of wives by force; it showed women acting for the good of the community rather than themselves; Livy uses it to contrast virtuous female behaviour with that of Tarpeia; the story grounded Rome's mixed racial origins in heroic myth.

practice_questions.text: How far do the myths of Pandora and Lucretia present women in the same way? Use named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10): A sustained argument comparing two or more named sources. Student identifies key similarities — both myths are shaped by male authors to police female behaviour — but also key differences: Pandora is presented as an innate threat created by the gods, while Lucretia's virtue makes her an active moral agent whose death triggers political change. Strong use of Hesiod (Works and Days 53–105) and Livy (1.57–59). May also bring in the Pudicitia statue as material evidence for Roman ideals. Clear, supported judgement reached.

Secure (7–8): Clear argument with comparisons of both myths, using named sources. Differences and similarities identified. Some source analysis. Supported judgement.

Developing (4–6): Some comparison made. One or both myths described but with limited analysis. Sources named but not deeply analysed.

Emerging (1–3): Mainly narrative retelling. Little comparison or source use.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Flight of Medea Krater presents Medea and what it reveals about Greek attitudes towards her.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6): The student accurately describes the krater (red-figure, c. 400 BC, Cleveland Museum of Art): Medea shown in her dragon chariot escaping, dead children visible below. They explain how the visual presentation emphasises her power (she escapes unpunished) and her transgression (she has killed her own children). They link this to Athenian anxiety about foreign women who defy social norms and act independently. Named source used throughout.

Secure (4–5): Accurate description of the main visual elements with explanation of what they reveal. Good connection to cultural context.

Developing (2–3): Some accurate description with limited analytical explanation.

Emerging (1): A simple descriptive point.

practice_questions.text: Name the Greek term for the longing to return home that drives Odysseus throughout the poem.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: nostos.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by an epithet in Homeric epic poetry, giving one example from the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a repeated descriptive phrase or fixed label attached to a character (or similar). 1 mark for a correct example, e.g. 'resourceful Odysseus' / 'godlike Odysseus' / 'rosy-fingered Dawn'. 1 mark for explaining its function: fills a metrical slot in the line / reinforces the character's defining quality / aids performance.

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of the opening of the Odyssey:

'The poet asks his Muse to sing of the resourceful man who wandered many years after the fall of Troy, suffering greatly on sea and suffering greatly on land, as he struggled to save his own life and the lives of his companions. Yet for all his striving, he could not save them — they were destroyed by their own recklessness.'

What does this opening passage suggest about the way Homer presents Odysseus and his companions? Refer to specific details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details from the passage with developed explanation of what they reveal about character or theme. Likely points: 'resourceful man' — the epithet immediately defines Odysseus by his intelligence and adaptability rather than strength; the contrast between Odysseus's survival and the crew's destruction establishes the theme of self-reliance; 'their own recklessness' — suggests the crew bear responsibility for their fate and signals the poem's interest in the theme of justice; the invocation of the Muse establishes epic authority and signals divine inspiration. Candidates who refer to specific words or phrases score more highly.
Secure: Two details identified and explained, without full analytical development.
Developing: One detail identified and explained.
Emerging: General comment on the passage with little specific reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the structure of the Odyssey — beginning in medias res — is effective for the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying in medias res correctly (the story starts in the middle of the action, with Odysseus already at sea for ten years). 1 mark for an effect on the audience (creates immediate drama / suspense / raises questions about the backstory). 1 mark for development (the earlier adventures are then told by Odysseus himself in Books 9–10, making him his own storyteller). 1 mark for linking to characterisation (this technique itself reveals Odysseus's skill with words and self-presentation).

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the oral tradition is the most important feature for understanding Homer's Odyssey? Refer to a range of named sources and give a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that engages with both sides. For: oral composition explains epithets (e.g. 'resourceful Odysseus'), formulae (reception scenes, set-piece descriptions), extended similes and structural repetition; understanding the tradition helps us interpret the text as a performance rather than a fixed literary work; the invocation of the Muse signals the poem's oral origins. Against: the poem's thematic richness — nostos, xenia, justice, civilisation vs barbarism — is independent of its oral origins; the sophisticated in medias res structure and the nested narrative of Books 9–12 show literary artistry; the prescribed books reward close reading regardless of oral context. Top answers will name specific episodes and technical features, and reach a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Two points on each side with at least one named source.
Developing: Mostly one-sided with limited source use.
Emerging: General discussion, few named sources, no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Homer uses language techniques to tell the story of the Odyssey effectively.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two techniques (e.g. epithets and extended similes, or formulae and in medias res), each with a specific example and developed explanation of effect. For epithets: fixed labels like 'resourceful Odysseus' signal character instantly and aid oral performance; for extended similes: comparing Odysseus attacking the suitors to a natural phenomenon grounds the heroic action in vivid, relatable imagery and slows the pace for dramatic effect.
Secure: Two techniques each with an example and a clear explanation.
Developing: Two techniques named but explanation limited; or one technique fully explained.
Emerging: General reference to 'language' without naming or explaining specific techniques.

practice_questions.text: Name the god associated with the sea and earthquakes in Greek religion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Poseidon.

practice_questions.text: Describe the statue of Zeus inside the Temple of Zeus at Olympia.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following details: the statue was chryselephantine (made of ivory and gold); Zeus was shown seated on a great throne; he was of enormous scale, with his head near the ceiling; he held a figure of Nike (Victory) in one hand; he held a sceptre topped with an eagle in the other; the sculptor was Pheidias.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following account of a Greek statue:

A twelve-metre figure of a goddess stood inside a great temple. She wore a helmet and held a small winged figure of Victory in her right hand, with a spear in her left. Her shield rested upright on the floor beside her, with her sacred snake coiled inside it. Every detail of the statue had meaning.

Using the passage and your own knowledge, explain what this statue tells us about how the Greeks represented their gods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Detailed analysis of at least three specific details from the source, linked to the wider significance of anthropomorphism and the goddess's specific attributes. Uses the source precisely (helmet = military role; Nike = victory; snake = Athena's sacred animal) and draws on knowledge of the Parthenon and Pheidias with accurate supporting detail. Evaluates what the visual choices reveal about Greek religion.
Secure (4): Analyses two or more details from the source with clear explanation of their significance. Some reference to broader context (the Parthenon, Pheidias, Athenian identity).
Developing (3): Identifies one or two specific details and attempts explanation; may be descriptive rather than analytical.
Emerging (1–2): General observations about the source with little analysis or use of own knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Explain why anthropomorphism was important to Greek religion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the concept (the gods take human form / look and behave like humans); 1 mark for explaining why it mattered (it made the gods relatable / meant worshippers could understand and communicate with them); 1 mark for a developed point about how this shaped art or ritual (gods shown in human poses in vase painting; cult statues given clothing and food); 1 mark for linking to a specific named source (e.g. Athena Parthenos, the Exekias cup showing Dionysos).

practice_questions.text: How important was the Olympian family of gods to ancient Greek religion and culture? Use a range of sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained argument engaging with multiple aspects of importance (governing all natural domains; structuring myths and festival; inspiring art and architecture; providing divine models of behaviour). Uses a range of named sources (Pheidias Zeus at Olympia; Athena Parthenos; Exekias Dionysos cup; Homeric Hymns; myth episodes). Evaluates relative importance with a supported judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear argument covering at least two aspects of importance with relevant named sources and some analysis.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points with basic source reference; explanation limited.
Emerging (1–2): Simple list of facts about the gods; sources absent or vague.

practice_questions.text: Give two symbols or attributes that identify Athena in Greek art.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: owl; helmet; spear; aegis (breastplate/shield with Gorgon head); olive branch or olive tree; figure of Nike.

practice_questions.text: Name one of the two main roads in a Roman town grid plan.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: cardo OR decumanus (either name accepted).

practice_questions.text: Describe what the forum of Pompeii looked like and how it was used.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for up to three accurate details: e.g. large open rectangular space / surrounded by a two-storey colonnade / Temple of Jupiter at the north end / basilica and magistrates' offices on the sides / statues of emperors and benefactors / centre for civic, commercial and religious life. No marks for vague generalities; each point needs a specific feature.

practice_questions.text: Read the following passage, which paraphrases Juvenal's Satire 3. In it, a man describes the miseries of living in Rome: the constant rumble of carts at night, the fear of falling masonry from badly built upper storeys, and buckets of waste hurled from windows above. What does this source tell us about life in a Roman city? What are its limitations as evidence?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the source (carts at night, falling masonry, waste from windows) and connects each to knowledge of Roman city conditions (ban on daytime wheeled traffic, poorly built insulae, lack of sanitation). Evaluates the source's limitations with precision — Juvenal is a satirist writing for a wealthy audience; he exaggerates for comic effect and represents only one viewpoint. Reaches a supported judgement about how useful the source is.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the source and links them to knowledge. Identifies at least one limitation (satire / exaggeration / limited viewpoint) with some explanation.
Developing: Picks out a detail or two and makes a general comment about limitations without full development.
Emerging: Paraphrases the source or makes very general points about Roman city life without engaging with the text.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the grid plan was a useful design for Roman cities.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a reason; 1 mark for explaining it. Up to two explained reasons for full marks. E.g.: Easy navigation (1) — a regular street pattern meant both residents and newcomers could find their way without getting lost, making trade and administration more efficient (1). Ease of expansion (1) — new blocks could simply be added to the existing grid, allowing the city to grow in an orderly way (1). Easy administration (1) — the regular layout made it simple to identify properties, collect taxes and maintain public buildings (1). Any two well-explained reasons score full marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful are Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence for everyday life in Roman cities? Use sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues with precision, using named sources (thermopolia, stepping stones, forum colonnade, inscriptions, Insula of Diana at Ostia for comparison). Evaluates both the value of the evidence (exceptional preservation, wide range of building types, commercial and domestic detail) and its limits (both are frozen in AD 79; both are Italian towns, not the capital; Pompeii may not represent the poorest Romans). Reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Uses two or more named examples from Pompeii or Herculaneum and makes a clear argument about usefulness, with at least one evaluative point.
Developing: Describes what Pompeii reveals but does not evaluate; argument is one-sided or unsupported.
Emerging: General statements about Pompeii without named evidence.

practice_questions.text: How far do the physical remains of Pompeii give us a complete picture of Roman city life? In your answer, refer to both the evidence and its limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument using a range of named sources (e.g. thermopolia, forum layout, stepping stones, wall-paintings, graffiti inscriptions, water tower/castellum aquae). Considers both strength of evidence (extraordinary preservation; wide range of building types; evidence from both wealthy and ordinary households) and limitations (single moment in time — AD 79; not the capital; limited evidence for the very poorest; bias towards surviving stone buildings). Reaches a supported judgement about how complete the picture is, perhaps noting that Ostia or literary sources like Juvenal fill some of the gaps.
Secure: Clear argument using several named examples; evaluates both strength and limitation; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes the evidence but does not evaluate it critically; argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging: General descriptive points about Pompeii without use of specific named evidence.

practice_questions.text: Name the prophetess who delivered Apollo's oracle at Delphi.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Pythia.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role and duties of the Vestal Virgins at Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: they tended the sacred flame of Vesta in her temple in the Roman Forum; they served for thirty years (ten training, ten active, ten teaching); they were recruited between the ages of six and ten from good families; they were freed from the authority of a male guardian; they could make wills and own property; a Vestal found guilty of breaking her vow of chastity was buried alive.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases a description of the Thesmophoria festival:

'For three days each autumn, the women of Athens left their homes and set up camps near a sanctuary. No man was permitted to enter. The women who could afford it paid for the animals to be sacrificed; others carried out the sacred rites connected with the earth and with the story of Persephone. The festival had to be organised and funded by the women themselves.'

What does this passage reveal about the religious roles available to Athenian women? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A thorough analysis that uses multiple specific details from the passage (e.g. the exclusion of men, the women's organisational and funding roles, the connection to Persephone's myth) and links them to the broader significance of the Thesmophoria as evidence that women had real religious agency and a sacred sphere entirely their own. Draws a supported judgement, perhaps noting the paradox of public religious authority alongside domestic confinement.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the passage and explains what each reveals about women's religious roles. Makes a clear point about what this shows, such as that women could exercise genuine authority and initiative in a religious context.
Developing: Identifies one or two details from the passage and makes a basic observation about women's religious life, but the explanation of significance is limited or undeveloped.
Emerging: Mentions the passage in a general way without specific detail or explains it very briefly without engaging with significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the role of the Pythia was significant for our understanding of the status of women in the ancient Greek world.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying who the Pythia was (the prophetess of Apollo at Delphi). 1 mark for explaining what made her role significant (she influenced political decisions and military campaigns; rulers and city-states consulted her). 1 mark for contextualising this against the normal position of women (Athenian women were typically confined to the home and excluded from public life). 1 mark for a supporting detail (e.g. her identity was submerged in the god, suggesting her authority came from divine inspiration rather than personal status; she was drawn from ordinary women).

practice_questions.text: How far do the religious roles of women in Greece and Rome suggest that women had real power in the ancient world? Use a range of named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, well-structured argument that engages with the key tension: religious roles gave women real authority and public visibility, but this power was bounded, conditional, and defined by purity. Uses named sources from both cultures (Pythia, Thesmophoria, Parthenon Frieze for Greece; Vestal Virgins, Bona Dea rites, Temple of Vesta, Flaminica Dialis for Rome). Compares the two cultures fairly, noting that the Vestals' legal privileges went beyond Greece in giving women tangible civic rights. Reaches a supported judgement: religion gave women genuine power in specific, defined spheres, but this was not the same as equality with men.
Secure: Discusses examples from both cultures with relevant source references and makes a clear argument about the degree of power women held. Sustains an explanation throughout and offers a conclusion, even if not fully nuanced.
Developing: Covers some relevant material from one or both cultures but the argument is uneven. Sources may be named but not fully analysed. The conclusion may be asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: Makes general points about women and religion, possibly listing some roles without explaining their significance or using named sources consistently.

practice_questions.text: How similar were the religious roles available to women in Greece and Rome? Give at least two examples from each culture in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced comparison that identifies both similarities (both cultures had formal female priesthoods, both had female prophetesses whose words shaped state decisions, both had women-only sacred rites) and genuine differences (Vestals had legal privileges beyond the religious sphere; Greek ritual mourning and the Thesmophoria gave women control over important communal rites). Uses named examples from each culture (Pythia, hiereia, Thesmophoria for Greece; Vestal Virgins, Bona Dea, Sibyls, Flaminica Dialis for Rome). Reaches a supported conclusion.
Secure: Gives two clear examples from each culture, identifies at least one similarity and one difference, and supports with named evidence.
Developing: Gives examples from both cultures but the comparison is limited; similarities or differences may be implied rather than stated directly.
Emerging: Covers one culture in more detail than the other, or lists roles without comparing them.

before.exam_tip_html: When a question uses the command word ‘Describe’ for a priestess or festival, give at least three factual details: what the person or festival was, where it took place, and what specific role women played. The examiner rewards precise knowledge. When the question asks you to ‘Explain’ or ‘Analyse’ a source, resist simply narrating what it shows — push to say what it reveals about the status of women or the culture’s values. The most common error in essays on women and religion is over-generalising: students write “women had no power” when the evidence of the Vestals and the Pythia shows the opposite. Use named sources (Parthenon Frieze, the Vestal’s House, Plutarch) to support every claim.

practice_questions.text: Name one room found in a Roman bath complex.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: apodyterium / tepidarium / caldarium / frigidarium / palaestra.

practice_questions.text: Describe the hypocaust system used to heat Roman baths.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as an underfloor heating system; 1 mark for explaining that a furnace (praefurnium) heated air in a hollow space beneath a raised floor resting on brick pillars (pilae); 1 mark for noting that hot air also passed through hollow wall tiles (tubuli), heating the room from all sides.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which describes a visit to the Forum Baths at Pompeii:

'The bather first left his clothes in the changing room, placing them in one of the niches set into the wall. Moving into the warm room, he felt the gentle heat rising through the tiled floor. In the hot room beyond, thick clouds of steam gathered near the ceiling, and the bather sweated freely before a slave scraped the oil and grime from his skin.'

What does this passage suggest about how Romans bathed? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the source (e.g. niches for clothes, warm room, hot room, oil scraped by slave) to build a sustained analysis of bathing practice and what it reveals about Roman social life, including the role of slaves or the sequence of rooms. Evidence from other sources used to add context.
Secure: Identifies two or more details from the source and explains what they reveal about Roman bathing, with some contextual knowledge of the room sequence or the strigil.
Developing: Identifies one detail from the source and offers a limited explanation; may paraphrase rather than analyse.
Emerging: Describes the passage without analysis; little or no use of specific detail from the source.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Roman baths were important in the social life of a Roman city.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per developed point (up to 4). Points may include: the baths were a place where people from different social classes met (1); admission was cheap or free, making them accessible to most citizens (1); people conducted business, socialised and exercised there as well as washing (1); politicians sponsored free bathing as a way of winning popular favour (euergetism) (1); they provided a space for physical exercise through the palaestra (1). Accept other well-supported points.

practice_questions.text: How useful are the remains of the Forum Baths at Pompeii as evidence for Roman bathing habits? In your answer, refer to what the building can and cannot tell us.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument weighing the value of the physical remains (preserved room sequence, hypocaust, decoration, separate men's and women's sections) against their limitations (can't show frequency of use, personal experience, or the perspective of slaves and women). Draws on literary sources (Seneca, Horace) for comparison.
Secure: Identifies at least two things the Forum Baths reveal AND acknowledges at least one limitation; some reference to literary sources.
Developing: Mostly describes the Forum Baths without evaluating their usefulness; little acknowledgement of limits.
Emerging: Brief, descriptive answer with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: 'The Roman baths were primarily a place for hygiene rather than socialising.' How far do you agree with this view? Use evidence from literary and material sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument weighing both sides. Argues that physical design (room sequence, hypocaust) does point to a hygienic function, but draws on Seneca's Epistulae Morales, Horace's Satires and the layout of the Forum Baths to demonstrate that the baths were equally or more importantly a social, political and commercial space. Reaches a supported judgement with named sources.
Secure: Clear argument with reference to at least two named sources (one literary, one material); both sides addressed and a conclusion reached.
Developing: Makes some relevant points about social and hygienic functions but evidence is limited or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple points with little evidence; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Give the name of the Spartan state education and training system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: agoge; 1 mark for a relevant detail (e.g. boys entered at age seven / run by the state / compulsory for all Spartan boys who wished to become citizens).

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Spartan bronze warrior figure (British Museum) shows and what it suggests about Spartan values.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific visual detail (muscular male figure / right arm raised / in dynamic forward motion); 1 mark for a second visual or material detail (compact, energetic posture / small bronze votive figurine); 1 mark for what it reveals about Spartan values (celebration of the warrior body in action / idealisation of military aggression / the warrior ideal as central to Spartan religious and civic life).

practice_questions.text: Below is a paraphrase of part of Tyrtaeus Fragment 10. A Spartan poet describes the ideal warrior: it is a beautiful thing for a brave man to fall and die in the front rank, fighting in defence of his city. The man who plants his feet and holds firm — who does not think of flight — is the truest kind of hero. Analyse this source as evidence for the Spartan idealisation of war.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Uses specific details from the passage (dying in the front rank, holding firm, rejection of flight) to make analytical points about Spartan values; explains what each detail reveals (e.g. dying in battle as the highest honour, not running as a core value of the agoge, etc.); places the source in its cultural and literary context; sustains analysis throughout. Secure: Identifies relevant features and makes valid analytical points; some explanation of significance. Developing: Describes the passage rather than analysing it; limited explanation of what it reveals about Spartan society. Emerging: Simple observations with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the syssitia strengthened the Spartan military.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid point with explanation, up to 4: the syssitia created bonds of loyalty and trust between warriors who ate and slept together / compulsory membership meant all Spartiates shared the same experience regardless of personal wealth / exclusion for non-contribution meant the system enforced solidarity / the shared eating group became the basic unit of battlefield loyalty / the system extended the agoge’s discipline into adult life.

practice_questions.text: How important was the agoge in creating the Spartan military system? Use sources to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that evaluates the agoge’s importance while also considering other factors (the syssitia, the helot system, the warrior ideology expressed in Tyrtaeus, the krypteia, the perioeci); uses named sources; reaches a clear, supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument addressing the agoge alongside at least one other factor; uses some named sources; judgement present. Developing: Addresses the agoge in some detail but limited engagement with other factors; uses sources selectively; judgement may be underdeveloped. Emerging: Describes the agoge but little argument; limited sources; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the helot system was essential to Spartan military power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that helot agricultural labour freed Spartiates from working the land; develops this to show that continuous military training required economic support the helots provided; discusses the risk this posed (helots vastly outnumbered Spartiates, making the krypteia and military vigilance necessary); uses named sources or examples. Secure: Clear explanation of the helot system and its military significance; some development. Developing: Basic explanation; limited connection to the wider military system. Emerging: Vague or limited explanation; few relevant points.

practice_questions.text: What is a libation?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a liquid offering (wine, water, milk or oil) poured out as an act of worship to the gods.

practice_questions.text: Describe how an animal sacrifice was carried out in ancient Greece.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the animal was led in procession to the altar adorned with garlands; water and barley grains were scattered and the animal's 'consent' obtained; the animal was killed at the altar and the blood poured over it; the internal organs were inspected for omens; the thighbones and fat were burned on the altar fire as the gods' share; the remaining meat was roasted and eaten by the community.

practice_questions.text: Consider this description of a scene painted on a Greek vessel: a procession of figures approaches a stone altar; the leading figure holds a vessel from which liquid is being poured onto the altar's surface, while others carry garlands; in the background an ox is being led forward with gilded horns. What does this scene tell us about how the Greeks worshipped? Use specific details from the description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Uses multiple specific details from the description (liquid poured on altar = libation; garlands on figures and gilded horns on ox = ceremonial preparation; procession = communal public event) with sustained analysis linking each to what it reveals about Greek religious attitudes (reciprocity, spectacle, community, the god's share vs the people's share). Judgement clearly expressed.
Secure (3-4): Two or three details analysed with clear explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description of sacrifice without engaging with source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why animal sacrifice was so important in both Greek and Roman religion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following: sacrifice was the most valuable gift a worshipper could give, reflecting the 'do ut des' logic; it was a public communal event that reinforced civic bonds; it provided meat for the community, making it an important social occasion; it gave religious officials an opportunity to read omens from the entrails; it maintained the gods' goodwill through regular, correct performance of ritual; it was tied to festivals and calendar events so structured the religious year.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that animal sacrifice was the most important form of worship in the ancient Greek and Roman world? Use a range of named sources and a balanced argument.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained balanced argument weighing sacrifice (public ritual, meat feast, divination, civic bonding) against other forms of worship (household lararium, votive offerings, prayer, libations) with specific named examples; awareness that 'importance' can mean different things (public vs private piety; elite vs everyday worshipper); judgement clearly supported by named sources and evidence.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument covering at least two forms of worship with named evidence and a conclusion.
Developing (3-5): Some relevant points; limited comparison or limited source use.
Emerging (1-2): Simple descriptive points; little argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Greek and Roman animal sacrifice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Roman priest covered head capite velato vs Greek bare-headed; Roman haruspex examined entrails formally vs Greek more informal; suovetaurilia in Rome vs more varied animals in Greece) each with a named example and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about each culture's attitudes to the gods.
Secure (3-4): Two differences explained with some evidence.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

practice_questions.text: Give two weapons carried by a Roman legionary into battle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct weapon up to two: gladius (short stabbing sword); pilum (heavy javelin); pugio (dagger). Accept accurate description if exact term not given.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Roman scutum and explain its importance in battle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three: the scutum was a large rectangular or semi-cylindrical shield; it was made from laminated wood covered in leather and linen; it curved around the soldier's body to protect his left side; the central metal boss could be used offensively to punch opponents; it was used collectively to form the testudo formation in sieges.

practice_questions.text:
Look at this description of a Roman material source: a tall marble column standing in Rome, decorated with a continuous spiral relief carving. The relief depicts scenes from a military campaign: soldiers constructing a camp by digging a ditch and piling up earth; legionaries marching in formation; artillery machines being operated; a commander addressing his troops from a platform.

What does this source tell us about the Roman army? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis linking specific scene types (camp building, formation marching, artillery use, commander speech) to wider knowledge of Roman military practice. The response considers the source's purpose (imperial propaganda glorifying Trajan) alongside what it reveals, and acknowledges its limitations (official version, not a neutral record). At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details from the source with accurate supporting knowledge. Some engagement with what the source reveals and what it might not show.
Developing: General reference to the source; mainly descriptive; limited analytical comment.
Emerging: Minimal engagement; knowledge vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pilum was such an effective weapon against enemy formations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: the pilum's long iron shank bent on impact, preventing the enemy from throwing it back; if it hit a shield, the bent shaft weighed the shield down, forcing the enemy to drop it; this left the opponent exposed just before the Romans closed with their gladii; a simultaneous volley of pila from a century created shock and disorder in the enemy line at the critical moment.

practice_questions.text: How effective was Roman military equipment in giving the legionary an advantage over his enemies?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis covering multiple pieces of equipment (pilum, gladius, scutum, lorica segmentata) and explaining precisely how each gave a tactical advantage. The response also considers limitations (enemy adaptations, terrain limitations) and uses named sources. A supported conclusion is reached.
Secure: Clear argument covering at least two pieces of equipment with developed explanations. Mostly sustained.
Developing: Some relevant points but limited range or development.
Emerging: Simple descriptive points; limited argument.

practice_questions.text: How important was Roman engineering skill to military success? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument evaluating engineering as a core Roman military advantage, covering camp-building (daily fortification on campaign), siege equipment (ballistae, approach ramps), bridge-building, and the construction of permanent fortresses. The response sets this against other factors (equipment quality, unit discipline, tactical flexibility) and reaches a supported judgement. Named sources (Trajan's Column, Chester fortress, Vegetius) are integrated as evidence.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Some range of points and a supported conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points; limited range or one-sided argument.
Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited; may retell without arguing.

practice_questions.text: What was the main purpose of a basilica in a Roman city?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a law court / venue for legal proceedings AND commercial business. Both functions are acceptable; one is sufficient for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the layout and appearance of the forum at Pompeii.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for up to three accurate features: e.g. large rectangular open space / paved with limestone / surrounded on three sides by a two-storey colonnade / Temple of Jupiter at the north end on a raised podium / basilica at the south-west corner / macellum at the north-east / statues of emperors and benefactors. Each point needs a specific feature, not a vague statement.

practice_questions.text: The following is a paraphrase of a Pompeian wall inscription (programmata): 'The fruit sellers, together with Helvius Vestalis, urge you to elect Marcus Holconius Priscus as duumvir for the administration of justice.' What does this inscription reveal about civic life in Pompeii? What are its limitations as evidence?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the inscription (fruit sellers as endorsers, the named candidate, the role of duumvir for justice) and links each to knowledge of Pompeian civic life — elections were competitive; tradespeople participated in politics; duumviri were the chief magistrates. Evaluates limitations clearly: inscription only represents those who could afford public notices; we do not know whether the candidate won; survivorship of inscriptions is random. Reaches a supported judgement about usefulness.
Secure: Uses at least two details and links them to civic life; identifies one limitation with explanation.
Developing: Makes general points about elections without engaging with specific details in the inscription.
Emerging: Paraphrases the inscription without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Temple of Jupiter was placed at the north end of the forum at Pompeii.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a reason; 1 mark for explaining it. E.g.: Position of honour (1) — placing the most important god at the head of the forum, dominating the space, showed that Roman civic life was under divine authority and that Jupiter’s approval was essential for the city’s success (1). Visibility (1) — the raised podium and elevated columns meant the temple could be seen the length of the forum, reminding all who entered of the god’s importance (1). Up to two explained reasons for full marks.

practice_questions.text: How do the public buildings of Pompeii reflect Roman civic values? Use named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues clearly using named examples (basilica, Temple of Jupiter, macellum, programmata, statues of benefactors, Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche inscription). Connects each to a Roman civic value: law and order (basilica), piety (Temple of Jupiter), organised commerce (macellum), civic participation (programmata), public generosity (benefactor statues/inscriptions). Makes a clear overall argument about what these buildings collectively tell us.
Secure: Uses two or more named examples and connects each to a civic value, with clear explanation.
Developing: Describes what the buildings looked like but does not develop the link to civic values.
Emerging: General statements about the forum without named sources.

practice_questions.text: How far do the public buildings of Pompeii show us that religion was central to Roman civic life?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument using a range of named sources. For religion's importance: Temple of Jupiter at the head of the forum; Temple of Apollo in its own precinct; Temple of Isis showing diversity of worship; religious imagery in civic buildings. Counter-argument: buildings also show commerce (macellum), law (basilica), and politics (programmata, magistrates’ offices) were equally central. Reaches a supported judgement, perhaps arguing that religion was inseparable from civic life rather than separate from it.
Secure: Uses several named examples, addresses both sides, reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes religious buildings without evaluating their relative importance; one-sided argument.
Emerging: General descriptions without specific named sources.

practice_questions.text: Name the Roman equivalent of the Greek god Hermes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Mercury.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Augustus of Prima Porta statue.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate details: it is a marble statue of Augustus; he stands in a military/oratorical pose with arm raised; he wears armour (a cuirass/breastplate); the breastplate shows a cosmic scene including the sky, earth and a military triumph; at the base is Cupid riding a dolphin (referencing Venus and Augustus's divine descent); found at Prima Porta near Rome; now in the Vatican Museum.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following description of a Roman monument:

A marble altar was enclosed by carved walls showing a solemn procession of the emperor, his family and priests. Other panels showed the goddess of Rome seated in armour, and the Trojan hero Aeneas making a sacrifice to the gods. The whole structure was built to celebrate a period of peace brought about by the emperor's victories.

Using the passage and your own knowledge, explain what this monument tells us about how the Romans used myth to express power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Detailed analysis of at least three elements from the source linked to wider argument: the procession shown alongside mythological scenes deliberately blends present and mythological past; Aeneas connects the emperor to Venus and Trojan lineage; ‘Rome seated in armour’ personifies the city as a divine protector; the peace celebrated is divine in origin. Uses the name Ara Pacis and provides specific contextual detail (built 13–9 BC, dedicated 9 BC; commissioned by Augustus). Evaluates what this reveals about Roman use of myth as political theology.
Secure (4): Analyses two or more details with clear explanation of the political/divine significance. Names the Ara Pacis and Augustus.
Developing (3): Identifies one or two details with some explanation; may describe rather than analyse.
Emerging (1–2): General comments about the monument with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Mars was more important in Roman religion than his Greek equivalent Ares was in Greek religion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the basic difference (Mars was second only to Jupiter; Ares was unpopular/mocked in Greek myth); 1 mark for explaining the cultural reason (Rome was a militaristic state built on conquest; war had divine prestige); 1 mark for a specific point about Mars (divine father of Romulus; protector of Roman armies); 1 mark for a comparison with Ares (shown as brutal and often defeated; mocked by gods including Athena).

practice_questions.text: 'The Romans simply copied the Greek gods and gave them new names.' How far do you agree with this view? Use named sources to support your argument.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10): Sustained argument engaging with evidence on both sides. Evidence for copying: same domains, myths retold (Ovid's Metamorphoses), same anthropomorphic representation in art. Evidence against: Mars vs Ares (cultural shift in prestige); Capitoline Triad (no Greek equivalent); pax deorum (ritual focus vs mythological focus); Augustus of Prima Porta and Ara Pacis as distinctly Roman political uses of divine imagery; Vesta's eternal flame; Apollo keeping his Greek name. Reaches a well-supported conclusion about the nature of Roman adaptation. Uses multiple named sources.
Secure (7–8): Clear argument on both sides with some named sources and a reasonable conclusion.
Developing (5–6): Some relevant points on both sides; sources limited or imprecise.
Emerging (1–4): One-sided or general response; sources absent.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of the pax deorum and explain why it mattered to the Romans.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying what the pax deorum was (the peace/goodwill between gods and Romans; maintained by correct ritual); 1 mark for explaining its importance (it guaranteed Rome's prosperity, military success and safety; its disruption would bring disaster).

practice_questions.text: What name is given to the style of masonry using enormous unmortered limestone blocks at Mycenae?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Cyclopean masonry.

practice_questions.text: Describe the appearance of the Lion Gate at Mycenae.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: two large upright jamb stones supporting a massive lintel (estimated at around twenty tonnes); above the lintel is a triangular relief panel; the relief shows two animals (lionesses or lions) rearing up; they flank a central tapering column that widens towards the top and rests on a decorated base; the heads of the animals are now missing; dated to around 1250 BC.

practice_questions.text:
Look at this description of the Lion Gate at Mycenae:

'Above the entrance, carved in relief, two powerful creatures face each other across a central upright. Their forepaws rest on the base of the column between them. The gateway itself is formed from slabs of enormous weight.'

What does this source tell us about the Mycenaeans? Use details from the description and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: simple point from the source (e.g. 'the stones were big') with no development.
Developing: uses one or two details from the source to make a basic point about Mycenaean power or craft; description rather than analysis dominates.
Secure: uses specific details from the source (the heraldic animals, the scale of the stones, the column) and connects them to knowledge of Mycenaean society — argues what the relief communicates about royal power; notes that the column may symbolise the palace; discusses the deliberate choice of the gate as a location for monumental art.
Mastering: detailed analysis of what the source reveals and what it does not, with knowledge of the context (c.1250 BC; oldest monumental sculpture in Europe; the deliberate defensive approach ramp; the parallel with Near Eastern heraldic imagery). Evaluates both what the source tells us and the limits of material evidence alone.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the layout of the citadels at Mycenae and Tiryns suggests the Mycenaeans were skilled military planners.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four points (or 2 marks each for two well-developed points): the ramp at both sites forces attackers to expose their unshielded right side to defenders on the walls; the Cyclopean walls at Mycenae are up to eight metres thick and their original height is unknown, making direct assault extremely difficult; the underground passage to the cistern at Mycenae ensured water supply under siege; the sally port at Mycenae allowed covert sorties without using the main gate; the corbelled galleries at Tiryns provided protected internal storage and troop space; the controlled entrance with a single main gate allows defenders to focus their forces.

practice_questions.text: How far do the fortifications at Mycenae and Tiryns suggest that Mycenaean rulers were primarily concerned with military defence? Use evidence from both sites in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: simple listing of features with little discussion of their purpose.
Developing: some attempt to connect features to military purpose, but the argument lacks balance and uses vague descriptions.
Secure: a two-sided argument using specific named features from both sites. Supports the view that defence was a primary concern (Cyclopean walls, ramp design, cistern passage, sally port, corbelled galleries). Challenges it by noting that the citadels also contained palaces, storerooms, cult areas and prestige monuments — suggesting they were centres of political, religious and economic power as well as military bases.
Mastering: a sophisticated, evaluative essay that uses named evidence from Mycenae and Tiryns, considers what the sources can and cannot tell us, and reaches a clear, justified judgement. Might note the parallel with Homer's image of great-walled cities ruled by powerful kings.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of the corbelled galleries at Tiryns and explain what they were used for.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for feature: the galleries run inside the thickness of the Cyclopean walls; they are constructed using corbelling, where stones project inward to form a pointed arch. 1 mark for use: storage of equipment and supplies, or protected space for troops during a siege.

before.exam_tip_html: When a source analysis question shows you a material source such as the Lion Gate, always describe it precisely first — what you can see, the material, the scale — before moving to interpretation. Examiners reward students who use specific details from the source rather than general background knowledge alone. For ‘Describe’ questions about Mycenae or Tiryns, name the specific features: the Lion Gate, the Cyclopean walls, Grave Circle A, the megaron. Avoid vague answers such as “it had big walls and a palace.”

practice_questions.text: Name one type of gladiator and one item of equipment they used.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming a gladiator type (murmillo / retiarius / thraex); 1 mark for a correct piece of equipment for that type (murmillo: large shield / gladius; retiarius: net / trident / manica; thraex: sica / small rectangular shield).

practice_questions.text: Describe the design of the Colosseum in Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying its shape (elliptical / oval); 1 mark for a specific structural detail (tiered seating / velarium / 76 entrances / hypogeum / four storeys); 1 mark for a second specific detail or a detail about its exterior decoration (three architectural orders on lower three levels: Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian).

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which is based on the design and use of the Colosseum:

'The enormous oval building rose four storeys high. At the front sat the senators, closest to the sand. Rows behind them held the equestrian class and then ordinary citizens. High at the back, in the shade of a great canvas awning, sat women and the poor. Below the sand, a network of tunnels and cages concealed what the crowd would soon see: beasts from across the empire, ready to be raised through trapdoors into the light.'

What does this passage suggest about Roman society and values? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Draws on at least three specific details from the passage to analyse what they reveal about Roman society: the seating hierarchy (senators front, women/poor at back) shows the social order was physically mapped in public spaces; the awning (velarium) as a concession to those with least status; the underground hypogeum and exotic beasts as demonstrations of imperial power and reach. Uses wider knowledge (e.g. political purpose of games, editors) to contextualise the source.
Secure: Identifies two details from the passage and explains what they reveal about Roman values or social structure.
Developing: Identifies one detail and offers a limited explanation; may describe rather than analyse.
Emerging: Paraphrases the passage without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Roman emperors and politicians sponsored gladiatorial games.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per developed point (up to 4). Points may include: to win popular favour and appear generous to the people (1); as a display of wealth and power (1); to provide entertainment as a political tool — Juvenal's 'bread and circuses' suggests keeping citizens distracted from political engagement (1); to demonstrate the reach of the empire through exotic animals (venationes) (1); a poor or stingy show risked public embarrassment, so quality mattered (1). Accept other well-supported points.

practice_questions.text: How far do literary sources help us understand Roman attitudes to gladiatorial games? Refer to specific sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighs the value and limits of literary sources. Values: Juvenal's 'bread and circuses' shows elite critical attitudes; Seneca's personal disgust at the midday shows gives a first-hand emotional response. Limits: both are educated upper-class men who may not represent the majority; neither gives the perspective of a gladiator or an ordinary spectator. Material evidence (the Colosseum's tiered seating) provides complementary information about social structure. A balanced conclusion.
Secure: References at least two named literary sources and acknowledges at least one limit of this type of evidence.
Developing: Describes one source; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Brief, general answer with no named sources.

practice_questions.text: 'The gladiatorial games reveal that Roman society valued violence above all else.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from literary and material sources to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument engaging with complexity. Agrees: the scale of the Colosseum (50,000 capacity), the elaborate design (hypogeum, velarium), venationes and midday executions all suggest violence was institutionalised as entertainment. However, challenges the claim: Juvenal and Seneca show educated Romans were critical; gladiators were not always killed; free volunteers chose to fight; the games served political and social functions beyond mere cruelty. Reaches a supported judgement using named sources (Colosseum, Juvenal, Seneca).
Secure: Addresses both sides with at least two named sources; clear argument and conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points; evidence limited or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple description with no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Name the Greek term for the male guardian who arranged an Athenian woman's marriage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: kyrios.

practice_questions.text: Describe the typical Athenian wedding ceremony.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: the bride dedicated childhood toys and a lock of hair to Artemis before the wedding; she bathed in sacred water; a torch-lit procession carried her from her father's home to her husband's; singing and hymns accompanied the procession; the anakalypteria (unveiling ceremony) was a central ritual act in which the groom lifted the bride's kalyptra (veil); the transfer of authority from father to husband was the central act.

practice_questions.text: Read the following description of part of a Spartan wedding ritual: The bride's hair was cut short; she was dressed in a man's cloak and sandals, and left alone in a darkened room for her husband to find her. Using this description and your wider knowledge, analyse what this ritual reveals about Spartan attitudes to marriage and gender.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): The student uses specific details from the description (hair cut, male clothing, darkness) to analyse the ritual as a transition ceremony marking a change in the woman's status. They connect this to Spartan society's unusual attitudes: Spartan women were associated with physical robustness and the ritual may have eased the young groom's transition. Student may contrast this with the Athenian torch-lit procession, where femininity and modesty were emphasised. Named context given; source details used throughout.

Secure (3–4): Good use of specific details from the description with some analytical comment about Spartan gender attitudes. Some wider contextual knowledge.

Developing (2): Some relevant points but largely descriptive.

Emerging (1): A simple point with minimal analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the education of Spartan girls was so different from that of Athenian girls.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of: Sparta's society was organised around military strength and producing warriors; Spartan girls trained physically to make them fit for childbirth and to produce strong sons; Athens prized female modesty and domestic virtue rather than physical strength; Athenian women were trained for household management and seclusion; the Spartan state needed physically robust mothers because men lived in communal barracks and were largely absent; Athenian citizenship law required legitimate heirs which led to stricter control of women.

practice_questions.text: How far does the evidence suggest that marriage in Athens was more restrictive for women than marriage in Sparta? Use named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): A sustained argument using at least two named sources. Strong answer might compare Athenian and Spartan practices systematically: the kyrios, the dowry system and the age gap in Athenian marriage versus later marriage ages, female athletics and property ownership in Sparta. Reference might be made to Livy (for context), Plutarch (on Spartan customs), or material evidence such as the Hegeso Stele (which shows the domestic ideal). Clear supported judgement: 'more restrictive' supported with specific evidence.

Secure (5–6): Clear argument with comparison of both systems. Named sources used. Judgement reached.

Developing (3–4): Some comparison made, one or both systems described but limited analysis.

Emerging (1–2): Mainly narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Athenian dowry system affected the lives of women.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6): Two well-developed points. For example: (1) the dowry transferred economic responsibility from father to husband, meaning the woman remained financially dependent on male relatives throughout her life; (2) the requirement to return the dowry on divorce gave women some protection against abandonment. A strong answer will connect both points to the broader theme of women's legal powerlessness in Athens, noting that women could not represent themselves legally.
