practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following developed points: the unburied dead were believed unable to cross into Hades, condemned to wander for a hundred years; the obligation to bury was a moral and religious duty on the family; without a coin for Charon the soul could not cross the underworld rivers; proper burial kept the dead from becoming restless spirits who might harm the living; burial rites maintained the family's social prestige and public identity; it is illustrated in Sophocles' Antigone where Antigone defies a king's order to ensure her brother's burial.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Greek and Roman approaches to death and burial were essentially the same? Use named sources and a balanced argument in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained balanced argument identifying genuine similarities (both required burial outside city walls; both had ritual laying-out of the body; both used grave goods; both had festivals for the dead; both placed coins for Charon) alongside real differences (Roman funeral clubs for the poor with no Greek equivalent; Roman use of ancestor masks in processions; Lemuria specifically for malevolent spirits vs Genesia for honoured ancestors; Roman cremation was common before inhumation became more common; stelai in Greece vs elaborate roadside tombs and mausoleums in Rome); evidence from named sources (Sophocles' Antigone, the Hegeso Stele, Parentalia and Lemuria); clear judgement.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument with evidence for similarities and differences and a conclusion.
Developing (3-5): Points about one side with limited comparison or source use.
Emerging (1-2): Descriptive account; little argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Roman festivals for the dead differed from the Greek festival of the Genesia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Lemuria aimed at appeasing potentially harmful lemures/spirits vs Genesia as a respectful commemoration of honoured ancestors; Parentalia as a private family event with public ceremonies at graves vs Genesia as a public festival; Roman civic dimension of the Parentalia with public ceremonies and closure of temples vs Genesia as a public festival day observed by families at their own graves; the duration of Parentalia — nine days — vs the Genesia which was a single-day event) each with named evidence and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about Roman vs Greek attitudes to the dead.
Secure (3-4): Two differences explained with some evidence.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

practice_questions.text: Name the ferryman of the Greek Underworld who carried the souls of the dead across the river.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Charon.

practice_questions.text: Describe the character of Hades' kingdom as presented in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate details from or connected to the Hymn: it is a dark realm beneath the earth; it is the realm of permanent death and loss; Persephone is seized and taken there against her will; it is governed by rules (eating food in Hades binds one to return); even the gods must negotiate with Hades (Zeus sends Hermes as a mediator); the pomegranate episode shows the Underworld has binding legal power; it is a place of grief for those left behind (Demeter’s famine).

practice_questions.text:
Read the following summary of an episode from a Roman poet's account of a visit to the Underworld:

A young man, his lyre in hand, descended through the darkness to plead for his dead wife. When he played before the king and queen of the dead, even the most hardened inhabitants of that grim place felt his grief. The tortured souls paused their sufferings to listen; the judges of the dead were moved. The king agreed to release the young man's wife on a single condition, which would prove impossible to keep.

Using the passage and your own knowledge, explain what this episode tells us about Roman ideas of the Underworld and the power of love.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Analyses at least three specific elements of the source with precise own-knowledge support. Identifies this as Ovid’s Metamorphoses 10.1–64; the hero is Orpheus and his wife is Eurydice. ‘Even the tortured souls paused’ = the Underworld in Ovid is responsive to human emotion in a way that Greek sources often don’t show; ‘the judges of the dead were moved’ = the power of art and love temporarily overcomes divine law; the ‘condition impossible to keep’ = Orpheus’s fatal glance back; the Underworld’s rules are absolute even when bent by beauty. Evaluates what this reveals about Ovid’s Roman portrayal of the Underworld as humanised and emotionally rich, contrasting with the darker Greek version in the Hymn to Demeter.
Secure (4): Analyses two elements; names Ovid and Orpheus; some comment on what the episode reveals.
Developing (3): Identifies one or two details; largely descriptive.
Emerging (1–2): Retells the story with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Homeric Hymn to Demeter links the story of Persephone to the natural world.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining Demeter’s role (goddess of the harvest, responsible for crops and fertility); 1 mark for explaining what happened when she stopped (she abandoned her divine role, causing famine and drought); 1 mark for the pomegranate compromise (Persephone spends one third of the year below and two thirds above; the myth links Demeter’s grief and recovery to the fertility of the earth); 1 mark for the wider significance (the myth ‘explains’ the cycle of the seasons through a divine story of loss and partial recovery; it shows Greek religious thought connecting natural phenomena to divine action).

practice_questions.text: How similar are the Greek and Roman accounts of the Underworld and journeys to it? Use named sources to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained argument comparing both cultures. Similarities: both share the same geography (rivers, ferryman Charon, three-headed guardian Cerberus, ruler Hades/Pluto and Persephone, regions for different souls); both involve journeys by exceptional figures (Heracles, Orpheus/Persephone); both use the Underworld as a frame for exploring death, loss and the possibility of return. Differences: the Hymn to Demeter presents a harsh, legally rigid Underworld where even Zeus must compromise; Ovid’s Underworld is emotionally responsive (Hades and Persephone weep; punishments pause); the Roman version tends to humanise the Underworld more. Heracles in both cultures = mortal mastery over death = apotheosis. Uses named sources (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 1–104, 301–474; Ovid Metamorphoses 10.1–64). Reaches a supported conclusion.
Secure (5–6): Covers both similarities and differences; names both sources; clear argument.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant comparisons; limited source use.
Emerging (1–2): Describes one myth without comparing.

practice_questions.text: Give two rules or conditions that governed the Underworld in ancient Greek and Roman myth.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: the dead must pay Charon to cross (coin placed in the mouth or on the eyes); anyone who eats food in the Underworld is bound to return (pomegranate rule; Persephone); a living person who enters must not look back when leaving (Orpheus); those not properly buried must wait 100 years before Charon takes them; Cerberus prevents the living from entering and the dead from leaving.

before.exam_tip_html: The Underworld is rich in source material: the Homeric Hymn to Demeter and Ovid’s Metamorphoses 10.1–64 are both prescribed texts. For source analysis questions, make sure you can pick out specific details from the passage and link them to wider meaning. For the Hymn to Demeter, the key points are the nature of Demeter’s grief (she abandons her divine role, causing famine — shows how deeply the gods are tied to the natural world) and the compromise of the pomegranate (explains the seasons through a legal ruling in the Underworld). For Orpheus, the key point is the moment of looking back — explain both the literal failure (the condition was broken) and the deeper meaning (love cannot follow rules; the Underworld’s laws are absolute). Always avoid simply retelling the myth — examiners reward analysis of what the myth reveals about ancient beliefs.
